How much over the limit may you go while passing?","fact_ids":["sec05-R02"]},"answer":{"text":"Up to ten miles per hour over the limit, only while passing.","fact_ids":["sec05-R02"]},"rationale":{"text":"The allowance applies only on two-lane highways posted at fifty-five or more and only during a lawful pass.","fact_ids":["sec05-R02"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Position and pace","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Keep right","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03"]},{"text":"The basic speed law","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03"]},{"text":"Default speed limits","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Minnesota's traffic laws apply to everyone who drives on a public road anywhere in the state. This unit starts with two of the most basic: where you place your vehicle on the road and how fast you drive. You will learn the keep-right rule and the situations that allow you to leave the right side, the basic speed law, minimum speed limits, the three default limits that apply when no signs are posted, the special passing allowance, school and work zones, and why speed matters so much. Outside those situations, the right side of the road is where you belong. Driving faster than the posted limit is illegal, and on a road with a posted minimum speed, driving below it under normal conditions is illegal too. So there are two limits to keep in mind: the posted maximum, which you never exceed, and the speed that conditions allow, which may be lower. When conditions are poor, the reasonable speed is the lower of the two.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Three default limits","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-R01","sec05-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Ten in alleys","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-R01","sec05-F08"]},{"text":"Thirty on urban or town roads","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-R01","sec05-F08"]},{"text":"Fifty-five elsewhere","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-R01","sec05-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"When no signs say otherwise, Minnesota uses three default speed limits under ideal conditions. In alleys the limit is ten miles per hour. On urban or town roads it is thirty miles per hour. Everywhere else not otherwise listed, it is fifty-five miles per hour. Posted signs override all three. In a school zone you must slow down when children are present, and in a work or construction zone you must slow down and drive carefully. On two-lane highways posted at fifty-five miles per hour or higher, you may go up to ten miles per hour over the limit, but only while lawfully passing another vehicle. The trap is treating this as a general allowance. It does not apply on other roads, it does not apply when you are simply keeping up with traffic, and it ends as soon as the pass is complete. If a question mentions going over the limit, check that the road is a two-lane highway posted at fifty-five or more and that the driver is in the middle of a lawful pass.","fact_ids":["sec05-R02","sec05-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s6","kind":"bridge","title":{"text":"Why speed matters","fact_ids":["sec05-R03","sec05-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Less time to react","fact_ids":["sec05-R03","sec05-R04"]},{"text":"Higher crash and injury risk","fact_ids":["sec05-R03","sec05-R04"]},{"text":"Speeding loses right-of-way","fact_ids":["sec05-R03","sec05-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"The speed rules exist because driving faster shortens the time you have to react, raises the odds of a crash, and makes serious injury or death more likely when a crash happens. In other words, if you are speeding and another driver pulls out, you cannot claim the right-of-way you would normally have. Keeping to a lawful, reasonable speed protects you physically and legally at the same time.","fact_ids":["sec05-R03","sec05-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s7","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the passing allowance","fact_ids":["sec05-R02","sec05-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Two-lane highway posted fifty-five","fact_ids":["sec05-R02","sec05-F03"]},{"text":"Lawfully passing","fact_ids":["sec05-R02","sec05-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you are lawfully passing a slow vehicle on a two-lane highway posted at fifty-five miles per hour. On two-lane highways posted at fifty-five or higher, you may go up to ten miles per hour over the limit, but only while lawfully passing. So the answer is up to ten over, and only for the duration of the pass. Once you are back in your lane, the posted limit applies again, along with the basic speed law that keeps your speed reasonable for conditions.","fact_ids":["sec05-R02","sec05-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s8","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Position and pace recap","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-F08","sec05-R01","sec05-R02","sec05-R03","sec05-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Keep right, five exceptions","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-F08","sec05-R01","sec05-R02","sec05-R03","sec05-R04"]},{"text":"Basic speed law and minimums","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-F08","sec05-R01","sec05-R02","sec05-R03","sec05-R04"]},{"text":"Ten, thirty, fifty-five; ten over when passing","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-F08","sec05-R01","sec05-R02","sec05-R03","sec05-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"To sum up, Minnesota's traffic laws cover every driver on public roads. You will also see one more reason to keep your speed down, which has to do with how much of the road around you that you can actually see.","fact_ids":["sec05-F09","sec05-F10","sec05-F11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Fines and revocation","fact_ids":["sec05-F09","sec05-F10","sec05-R05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Extra fines at twenty over","fact_ids":["sec05-F09","sec05-F10","sec05-R05"]},{"text":"Over one hundred: revocation","fact_ids":["sec05-F09","sec05-F10","sec05-R05"]},{"text":"At least six months","fact_ids":["sec05-F09","sec05-F10","sec05-R05"]}],"narration":{"text":"You can be fined for driving faster than the posted speed limit, and additional fines apply if you drive twenty miles per hour or more over the limit. This unit covers how far ahead to signal and how long to keep signaling, when hand and arm signals may be used, why you must stay within a single lane even when the lines are faded or missing, how to change lanes safely, and what blind spots are, including the blind spots of other drivers. These are basic skills, but they are tested often because so many crashes start with a missed signal or a lane change into an unseen vehicle.","fact_ids":["sec05-F16","sec05-F18","sec05-F20"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Signal early, signal long","fact_ids":["sec05-F16"]},"lines":[{"text":"At least one hundred feet before turning","fact_ids":["sec05-F16"]},{"text":"Keep signaling until finished","fact_ids":["sec05-F16"]}],"narration":{"text":"When you want to change lanes or make a turn, use your signal to inform other drivers. Turn on your signal at least one hundred feet before you turn, and keep it on until the turn or lane change is finished. That distance gives drivers behind you time to see your plan and adjust their speed. A signal flicked on at the last moment does not give anyone enough warning, and one switched off too early leaves people guessing. Make it a habit to signal well before the corner and to check that the signal has stayed on through the whole move.","fact_ids":["sec05-F16"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Hand and arm signals","fact_ids":["sec05-F17","sec05-R07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Daylight only","fact_ids":["sec05-F17","sec05-R07"]},{"text":"Along with or instead of turn signals","fact_ids":["sec05-F17","sec05-R07"]},{"text":"Not when your hand is hidden","fact_ids":["sec05-F17","sec05-R07"]}],"narration":{"text":"During daylight hours you may use hand and arm signals in addition to or instead of your turn signals. You may not use hand signals at night, and you should not use them when driving a vehicle that blocks other drivers from seeing your hand. So hand signals are a daylight option, useful if a turn signal fails, but at night or in a vehicle where your arm cannot be seen, you must rely on the vehicle's turn signals. If your turn signals stop working, have them repaired, because every turn signal on the vehicle must work.","fact_ids":["sec05-F17","sec05-R07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Lanes, lane changes and blind spots","fact_ids":["sec05-F18","sec05-F19","sec05-F20","sec05-R13"]},"lines":[{"text":"Lanes exist marked or not","fact_ids":["sec05-F18","sec05-F19","sec05-F20","sec05-R13"]},{"text":"Space all around before moving","fact_ids":["sec05-F18","sec05-F19","sec05-F20","sec05-R13"]},{"text":"Turn your head; mirrors miss spots","fact_ids":["sec05-F18","sec05-F19","sec05-F20","sec05-R13"]}],"narration":{"text":"A traffic lane exists whether or not it is marked, and you must stay inside one lane without weaving or straddling the markings.
